restatements.text: Allows parents of a child eligible for public school to open an education savings account, into which the state must deposit 90 percent of the per-pupil funding the child's resident district would otherwise receive.
Permits the funds in the account to be used for private school tuition, tutoring, textbooks, and approved online courses.

analysis.answer: Current law pays state education funds only to public school districts and charter schools. The measure allows 90 percent of a student's public per-pupil funding to be diverted into an education savings account for alternative educational expenses.

The state shifts 90 percent of per-pupil funding from public schools to private accounts for participating students. Total state costs will likely increase if students who already attend private schools or are homeschooled open accounts, as the state currently spends nothing on their education.

Families choosing private or home education benefit from new state funding. Public school districts bear the cost of lost per-pupil revenue, which may not align with their ability to reduce fixed operational costs. Private schools and educational vendors benefit from the newly available funds.

Private schools and tutoring services may increase their tuition and fees or expand capacity to capture the new public funds. A higher number of families may shift away from public schools to alternatives. Public districts facing revenue losses might have to consolidate facilities or cut programs.

The measure addresses parent demand for broader school choice and control over educational spending by providing direct public funding. It risks creating public school funding shortfalls and could encourage the entry of low-quality educational providers seeking state funds.
Parents gain significant discretion over how their child's education funds are spent. Private schools, tutoring companies, and providers of online courses gain access to public funding.

The effect of education savings accounts and vouchers on student outcomes and public school finances is disputed. Some studies find improved outcomes and positive competitive effects, while others show negative test score impacts for participants and financial strain on public school districts.

Administration will require an agency or contractor to manage the financial accounts, verify that expenditures meet the eligible categories, and approve online courses, absorbing a portion of state resources.

flags.note: The text does not specify who approves the online courses or what standards apply.
The real effect of permitting funds for online courses depends on a future administrative process to approve them.
